title: Verified Jacobi Symbol Computation via Quadratic Reciprocity
description: Implementation of the Jacobi symbol algorithm as a recursive function in Lean 4, using quadratic reciprocity for reduction. Includes sign factor functions, strip2 decomposition, and concrete verifications.

overview.historicalContext: The Law of Quadratic Reciprocity, first proved by Gauss in 1796 (published in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, 1801), is often called the 'golden theorem' of number theory. Gauss himself gave six proofs. The law states that for distinct odd primes $p, q$: $(p/q)(q/p) = (-1)^{(p-1)/2 \cdot (q-1)/2}$. Combined with the two supplementary laws ($(-1/p) = (-1)^{(p-1)/2}$ and $(2/p) = (-1)^{(p^2-1)/8}$), this yields a GCD-like algorithm for computing Legendre and Jacobi symbols. The algorithm mirrors the Euclidean algorithm: at each step, either extract a factor of 2 (applying the second supplementary law), or swap numerator and denominator (applying reciprocity), reducing the first argument. Jacobi extended the symbol to composite odd moduli in 1837, and the resulting Jacobi symbol computation is used in primality testing (Solovay-Strassen test) and cryptographic applications. This formalization answers the open question from the parent proof: can the full computation be implemented as a verified recursive function with a termination proof in Lean 4?
overview.problemStatement: Implement the Jacobi symbol algorithm as an explicit recursive function in Lean 4 with a formally verified termination proof, and prove it equals Mathlib's `jacobiSym` and `legendreSym`. The algorithm should mirror the Euclidean algorithm: remove factors of 2 (supplementary law), swap via reciprocity, and recurse on the remainder.
overview.proofStrategy: The algorithm `jacobiAlgo a b flip ha` computes $J(a | b)$ (or $-J(a | b)$ when flip = true) via five cases: (1) if $4 \mid a$, divide by 4; (2) if $2 \mid a$, divide by 2 with sign from $(2/b)$; (3) if $a = 1$, return $\pm 1$; (4) if $a \mid b$, return 0; (5) swap via reciprocity to $(b \bmod a, a)$. Termination is proved by `termination_by a`: in cases 1-2, $a/4 < a$ or $a/2 < a$; in case 5, $b \bmod a < a$ — all via Nat.div_lt_self and Nat.mod_lt. Correctness is proved by strong induction (`Nat.strongRecOn`) mirroring the recursive structure, with each case using the corresponding Mathlib lemma (div_four_left, even_odd, quadratic_reciprocity_if). The `flip` boolean accumulates sign changes via XOR, avoiding intermediate $\pm 1$ multiplications.
keyInsights: The Jacobi symbol algorithm is structurally identical to the Euclidean algorithm: the first argument strictly decreases at every step (division by 2 or 4, or modular reduction), giving the same termination argument

The `flip` boolean accumulator is a functional programming technique that avoids intermediate sign multiplications: instead of computing $(-1) \cdot f(\ldots)$, pass $\text{xor}(\text{sign}, \text{flip})$ to the recursion and apply at the base case
The correctness proof by strong induction perfectly mirrors the recursive structure — each of the five algorithm cases corresponds to exactly one Mathlib lemma for the Jacobi symbol

The connection legendreCompute_eq bridges Mathlib's abstract legendreSym (defined via quotient types) with a concrete computable function, demonstrating that formal definitions can yield efficient algorithms
The `native_decide` tactic compiles the algorithm to native code and evaluates it during elaboration, giving verified computations like $(3/7) = -1$ essentially for free

sections.title: The Recursive Algorithm
sections.summary: Defines jacobiAlgo as a recursive function with five cases (remove factor of 4, remove factor of 2 with sign, base case a=1, divisibility check, QR swap). Termination proved by well-founded recursion on a, with three decreasing_by proofs.

sections.title: Correctness Proof
sections.summary: Proves jacobiAlgo_eq_jacobiSym: the algorithm equals Mathlib's jacobiSym (with sign from flip). Strong induction on a, five cases matching the algorithm, each using the corresponding Mathlib Jacobi lemma.

sections.title: Legendre Symbol Connection
sections.summary: Defines legendreCompute (reduces mod p, delegates to jacobiAlgo) and proves legendreCompute_eq: the algorithm computes legendreSym for odd primes, via jacobiSym.legendreSym.to_jacobiSym.

sections.title: Verified Example Computations
sections.summary: Seven concrete examples verified by native_decide: (3/7)=-1, (2/7)=1, (5/13)=-1, (7/11)=-1, (3/5)=-1, (2/17)=1, (6/7)=-1. Each annotated with mathematical explanation.

sections.title: Algorithm Properties
sections.summary: Proves jacobiAlgo_mod_left: the algorithm respects residue classes, J(a | b) = J(a mod b | b). Exports the three main results via #check.

conclusion.summary: This formalization provides a complete, verified implementation of the Jacobi symbol algorithm as an explicit recursive function in Lean 4. The algorithm mirrors the Euclidean algorithm, using quadratic reciprocity for the swap step and the supplementary laws for factor-of-2 extraction. All three main results — the algorithm itself with its termination proof, the correctness theorem equating it to Mathlib's jacobiSym, and the Legendre symbol corollary — are fully proved with zero sorries and zero axioms.
conclusion.implications: This demonstrates that classical number-theoretic algorithms can be faithfully implemented and verified in Lean 4, bridging abstract Mathlib definitions with concrete computations. The Jacobi symbol computation is foundational for computational number theory: it underlies the Solovay-Strassen primality test, the Tonelli-Shanks square root algorithm, and various cryptographic protocols. Having a verified implementation means these downstream applications can build on a trustworthy computational core.
openQuestions: Can the algorithm be extended to handle the full generalized Jacobi symbol for Gaussian integers or other number fields?
Can the Solovay-Strassen primality test be built on top of this verified Jacobi computation and proved correct in Lean 4?
Can the algorithm's computational complexity (O(log^2 n) bit operations, matching the Euclidean algorithm) be formally verified?
